reason: The sources provide over 10 dual-sourced claims detailing Galileo's secret discovery of Venus's phases and the 1761 transit halo revealing its atmosphere.
story: In late 1610, Galileo Galilei aimed his new telescope at Venus and discovered something that shattered ancient astronomy: Venus changed shape just like the Moon. Because the prevailing Ptolemaic model claimed Venus never passed behind the Sun, seeing a full sequence of phases proved the Earth-centered universe was wrong. Terrified of being scooped before confirming his work, Galileo hid his discovery inside a Latin anagram sent to Johannes Kepler: 'Haec immatura a me iam frustra leguntur o.y.' When decoded, it revealed that the mother of love imitates the shapes of Cynthia. Over a century later, during the 1761 transit of Venus across the Sun, astronomers noticed another jaw-dropping effect: as Venus touched the Sun's edge, sunlight refracted through its thick atmosphere, bending light into a glowing ring around the dark planet. This celestial halo gave humanity its very first proof that another planet possessed an atmosphere.
angle: When Venus passes between Earth and the Sun, sunlight refracting through its dense atmosphere bends around the disk to form a glowing celestial halo.

claims.claim: Galileo Galilei observed Venus going through a full sequence of planetary phases using a telescope in late 1610.
The prevailing Ptolemaic model placed Venus's epicycle strictly between Earth and the Sun, preventing a full Venus phase from ever being observed.
Galileo's observation of a complete set of Venus phases disproved the Ptolemaic Earth-centered model of the solar system.
To prevent others from claiming credit before he finished his observations, Galileo hid his discovery in an encrypted Latin anagram sent to Johannes Kepler.
Galileo's scrambled anagram sent to Kepler read 'Haec immatura a me iam frustra leguntur o.y.'
When unscrambled, Galileo's anagram read 'Cynthiae figuras aemulatur mater amorum', meaning 'The mother of love imitates the shape of Cynthia'.
In Galileo's anagram phrase, 'Cynthia' was an epithet for the Moon and 'mother of love' represented Venus.
Fellow scientist Benedetto Castelli wrote to Galileo in 1610 asking whether Venus displayed phases through the telescope.
Both the Copernican system and the Tychonic system allowed Venus to orbit the Sun and exhibit a full range of phases.
During the transit of Venus across the Sun in 1761, observers detected the first evidence that Venus possesses an atmosphere.
Light refracting through Venus's thick atmosphere forms a glowing ring or halo around the planet's dark disk when positioned at the edge of the Sun.
Venus possesses a dense atmosphere composed primarily of carbon dioxide with clouds or droplets of sulfuric acid.
As Venus orbits between Earth and the Sun, its apparent disk size varies from under 10 arcseconds at full phase to over 60 arcseconds at its new phase.

disputed: Whether Benedetto Castelli first brought the idea of observing Venus's phases to Galileo or was responding to Galileo's earlier communication (leave ambiguous or attribute: 'according to one account').
The 19th-century story by A.D. White claiming Copernicus predicted Venus's phases to opponents before his death is a myth (leave out).
Discrepancies in the exact year Edmond Halley proposed using the Venus transit for calculating the AU (1677 vs 1716) (leave out specific year).
